title: Compassion close
hook: compassion can grow, with practice and time

segments.voice: Yesterday: ten minutes of compassion, five people, one plain wish. Your line was may you be well. Who got it, silently, from you? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-three.

A farmer in the state of Song is worried. His grain is coming up too slowly. So he goes out into the field and, one by one, tugs every young stalk upward a little, to help it along. He comes home worn out and announces that he's been helping the crop grow. His son runs out to look. Every plant has withered. The philosopher Mencius tells this story, and it's a good one to end a stretch on, because this whole section has been about something that grows. Today closes the section on compassion, and asks how it grows.
screen: `A FARMER IN SONG.` → `TUGGING EVERY STALK.` → `THE WHOLE FIELD WITHERED.`

segments.voice: First, the sprout. Mencius, in the book that carries his name, says that anyone who suddenly saw a child about to fall into a well would feel alarm and distress, not for a reward, not for a reputation, simply because. In James Legge's translation he names that reaction plainly: "The feeling of commiseration is the principle of benevolence." He calls feelings like this beginnings, small shoots in every person that can grow or wither. Second, the farmer. Mencius says a sprout can be harmed two ways: by neglect, never weeding, or by yanking on it to hurry it. On his telling, goodness grows the way grain grows: tended, daily, without force. Third, the evidence, at its own scale. The research this path walked through points the same direction. Short programs measured gains in compassion. Weeks of loving-kindness moved one measure of bias. Real changes, modest in size, and some headlines along the way claimed far more, about the vagus nerve and the love hormone. It grows like grain, not like a magic bean. Fourth, the look back. The lines of this section: warmth, not drowning. Care for carers. Trainable. Wider. The seat. Not in a hurry. Be the one. For someone else. It spreads. Softer inside. Modest claims. Not so simple. Pass it on. Their side. The circle widens. Fierce and kind. Care heals. Me too. May you be well. A whole field of sprouts, none of them tugged.
screen: `A CHILD AT THE EDGE OF A WELL.` · `DON'T NEGLECT IT, DON'T TUG IT.` · `GRAIN, NOT A MAGIC BEAN.` · `A WHOLE FIELD OF SPROUTS.` · then, large: `IT GROWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk the field. Settle, and let the breath slow. Think back over this section, the last few weeks of practice. Look for one small change, the size of a sprout. A moment you wished someone well instead of drowning in their trouble. A seat you gave up. A kinder sentence to yourself after a mistake. Don't tug on it to make it bigger than it was. And if nothing comes, that's an honest answer too; it means keep weeding. When the bell ends, write the change down in one line. The bell holds the time.
Compassion close. The end of this section: compassion as a sprout, grown by tending, slowly, with practice and time. Today's word.
Your line: it grows. Today, keep the one line you wrote somewhere you'll see it again in a month, and don't tug. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: In the Confucian tradition, Mencius's "four beginnings" are taught as sprouts of goodness that grow through steady cultivation; some contemplative programs also ask people to keep a simple record of small changes over time.

fork.setup: in Mencius's story, the farmer of Song thinks his grain is coming up too slowly. what does he do?
options: tug every stalk upward a little, to help it along.
stop weeding, since nothing seems to work.
fork.reveal: he tugs every stalk, comes home proud, and the whole field withers. Mencius warns against both his mistake and its opposite, neglect.

original.note: Classical Chinese, from the Mencius: the heart of commiseration, one of his four beginnings.

trapdoor: what you thought: some people are compassionate and some aren't.
what it means: Mencius saw compassion as a sprout in everyone, grown by tending, not by force.
what a scholar hears: Mencius pairs the child at the well with the tugged grain: a beginning is given, and growing it takes patient, unforced work.

sources.quoted: The feeling of commiseration is the principle of benevolence

notes: Confirm the Legge wording of Mencius 2A:6: 'The feeling of commiseration is the principle of benevolence.' (Legge's Chinese Classics vol. 2.)

The child-at-the-well passage (2A:6) is paraphrased. Legge spells the state 'Sung'; the voice uses the pinyin 'Song'. The tugged-grain story is from 2A:2 and is paraphrased, including Mencius's two errors (neglect, not weeding; forcing, pulling up).
Confirm 惻隱之心 and the rough pronunciation (pinyin ce yin zhi xin).
The research recap restates earlier days' outline lines (1306, 1307, 1314, 1315) without new numbers.

Editor pass: the fork now asks what the farmer in the story does (the answer is his mistake, not advice); 'many contemplative programs' in howItsDone softened to 'some'. Note that 2A:2 is about nourishing the passion-nature (qi) through righteousness; 'goodness grows the way grain grows' is a fair gloss but a Keeper may check it.
